first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-mechanics problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and two independent inherited records (memory_86 on shortening onboarding, memory_31 on signup simplification) point at the same lever, which is the strongest convergent evidence available. That lever also compounds: it improves the yield of every acquisition channel rather than buying volume once. I verify memory_86 because it is the direct basis for the intended action and its summary reports completion and time-to-value gains without saying whether those accounts became qualified revenue — a shortened funnel can lift completion while stripping the qualification fields that make downstream accounts worth having, which would quietly damage the primary objective. I verify memory_73 because promotional pricing is the obvious reflex to the competitor's entry pricing and is the option most likely to look good and age badly: its summary claims acquisition and revenue lift but says nothing about margin, cohort retention, or whether the lift was durable past the promo window. Those two pulls maximally discriminate between the action I intend and the action I am most at risk of being pulled into. I am deliberately not treating these summaries as settled findings: all six are consolidated abstracts with the original conditions archived away, the oldest is 64 days stale, and none were measured under a competitor price shock, so their effect sizes may not transfer. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) and referral incentives (memory_57) are plausible but address neither declining metric and referrals amplify a funnel that is currently leaking. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the strongest fallback and becomes the choice if verification shows memory_86's gains came at the cost of lead quality. Running at standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, with retention, lead-quality, and downstream-conversion guardrails instrumented alongside the completion-rate headline, so that a completion lift that degrades qualified revenue is detectable rather than mistaken for success.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both questions in the direction that settles the decision. exp_86 held up cleanly and, importantly, on the dimension the summary had omitted: completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days came with 30-day retention +3%, so the funnel shortening did not buy completion by degrading downstream account quality. That is the compounding lever I wanted and it directly addresses two of the three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%). exp_73 failed exactly where I suspected the consolidated summary was hiding the cost: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% sat on top of 30-day retention -12%, and the original record explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The inherited memory_73 abstract had stripped that warning entirely, which is a caution about the other unverified summaries too. So promotional_pricing is now ruled out as a response to the competitor's entry pricing despite being the reflexive match to it — matching a price attack with a cohort that does not survive first renewal would actively damage the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Committing the slot to simplify_onboarding. Holding at standard_experiment rather than broad rollout: exp_86 was run under different conditions, before the competitor shock, and a 4% completion decline may have causes the prior treatment does not touch, so I want a clean measurement rather than an assumed replication. Instrumenting retention, lead quality, and downstream conversion alongside the completion headline so a repeat of the exp_73 failure mode — a good-looking top-line metric concealing cohort decay — would be visible rather than inferred later. memory_31 corroborates the direction and memory_91 (activation messaging) remains the sequenced follow-up if the onboarding lift does not carry through to activation; memory_44 and memory_57 stay unverified and unused, and referral incentives in particular should wait until the funnel stops leaking.
